A1.justification: Both PDFs describe First-Person Fairness in Chatbots. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support comparison. The new Appendix C and consequent renumbering can be matched reliably against retained material.

before.justification: v1 reports original chatbot-response experiments, human evaluation of LMRA ratings, post-training comparisons and analyses of public and private chat prompts.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds comparisons with external LMRA models and experiments using explicit demographic profiles.

M1.justification: Appendix C adds a direct-profile variant comparing explicit identities against a Canada-only profile. Its modified LMRA prompt identifies group-specific harmful content rather than matching responses to two demographic groups. The original name-based procedure and Bias Enumeration Algorithm remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix C substantially expands evaluated demographic conditions beyond name-associated binary gender and race, adding explicit non-binary, Hindu, Jewish, Muslim, hearing-impairment and visual-impairment profiles, alongside a female profile. These are simulated profile conditions tested on 12 existing tasks and all chats; the underlying datasets and original task coverage are retained.

E2.justification: New Table 2 adds six external graders to the human-agreement comparison: Llama 3.1 Instruct at 8B, 70B and 405B, Claude 3.5 Haiku and Sonnet, and Claude 3 Opus. This substantially expands comparison across evaluator families; these models are evaluated as LMRAs, not as additional target chatbots.

E3.justification: The added profile experiment introduces a shared 'I live in Canada' control, seven identity-bearing profiles and a 12-task subset plus all chats. The external-grader experiment specifies temperature 1 for Claude sampling. These are additional protocols; the original experiments' settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantive checks of two methodological dependencies: whether human agreement changes across evaluator families (Table 2), and whether name-based and explicit-gender measurements agree across tasks (Figure 15). Existing Memory-versus-Custom-Instructions, forward/reverse and post-training analyses remain.

E5.justification: Section 4.3 newly reports ten sampled completions from each Claude LMRA, adding repeated-sampling information for these ratings. Existing confidence-interval, significance-testing and Bonferroni practices remain unchanged. No increase in repetitions of the original experiments is established.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds evaluator-agreement results, while Figures 15–16 add direct-profile findings, including a reported name/direct-profile correlation of 0.98. Table 1 revises the Black–White human–LMRA correlation from 0.76 to 0.67, retaining 74.0% alignment. Original plotted results are retained. The new direct-profile magnitude comparison is internally inconsistent between Figure 15 and its description.

T1.justification: Section 3.3, Equation (2), corrects the reverse-rate definition: v1 evaluates groups in order (B,A) and equates this to the swapped-group forward rate; v2 retains (A,B) and measures selection of the B-response. This is a substantive local mathematical correction, beyond the accompanying notation changes.

C1.justification: The revised abstract explicitly claims the first large-scale fairness evaluation based on real-world chat data, a priority claim absent from v1. The central contributions concerning first-person bias measurement, human corroboration and mitigation through post-training remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the external-grader comparison as offering no substantial overall agreement advantage and presents direct profiles as extending applicability beyond names. Appendix H connects the travel-domain exception to restaurant-ethnicity matching. However, the new interpretation that direct profiles produce lower harms conflicts with Figure 15's labeled values.

D1.justification: v2 supplies the eight exact profile strings, their modified grading template, external evaluator configurations and Claude sampling settings. The introduction newly discloses review of published LMRA outputs for privacy. Existing system prompts, private-data restrictions and limitations on reproducing Memory behavior remain.

R1.justification: Related work adds Dhamala et al.'s BOLD dataset, Huang and He's clustering work, and Tamkin et al.'s Clio study, explaining their relationships to open-ended bias evaluation and usage analysis. Consolidating duplicate Cheng references does not remove a distinct cited work.

P1.justification: The abstract is condensed and rewritten, introductory privacy and contribution passages are revised, and Appendix C is inserted with subsequent appendices renumbered. Most methodological explanations, results discussion and existing appendix text remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds the evaluator-comparison table, two direct-profile plots and a grading-prompt box. Figure 9's caption gains an explanation of the signed rating scale. Existing figures are retained, with relocation, resizing and reflow rather than substantive redesign.

improvement.justification: Correcting Equation (2) improves the central metric's mathematical consistency, and Table 2 strengthens validation by comparing evaluator families against human judgments. These gains are tempered by reporting problems in the added profile study: Figure 15 contradicts its lower-harms claim, and Section 6 still states binary-gender-only coverage despite Appendix C. The net improvement is therefore limited.
